Memorandum dated May 10, 1972, from the Assistant Director, Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Department of the Interior.
Commenting on the proposed legislation, the memorandum asks for Comment: a discussion on the impact this expanded Federal authority would have on freedom States would have to regulate the taking of resident fish and wildlife. There would be some restriction of present State authority to regulate fish and wildlife. The Federal Government already has authority to regulate protection of some species and subspecies under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, Marine Mammal Act, Bald Eagle Act, and the Lacey Act. Those species remaining under State jurisdiction include most resident species consisting mainly of mammals, fishes, amphibians and reptiles. While the proposed legislation will expand the number of species and subspecies that will come under Federal protection, the actual number removed from State jurisdiction will be relatively small. Such jurisdiction can be delegated back to the State once the Secretary has determined that the State's program for that species or subspecies is adequate. Finally, once the goal, restoration of the species to a status no longer endangered, has been achieved the species can be removed from the endangered list and returned to State protection.
Comment: BLM also asks for an explanation of the present listing procedure and its categories to aid in understanding the new listing procedure.

Response: Present authority under the Endangered Species Conservation Act of 1969 provides for listing only species and subspecies threatened with extinction (endangered). The term "rare" and any species or subspecies so classified are not covered by that authority.
